subject: chemistry
title: Chemical Analysis Adventure: Pure, Mix, Chromatogram
welcome_lead: Today you'll tell pure from mixture and run paper chromatography.
meta_desc: GCSE Chemistry Chemical Analysis — pure substances, mixtures, formulations and paper chromatography basics.
final_note: You learned the chemist's meaning of pure, what a formulation is, and how to set up chromatography.

concepts.def: One element or compound — sharp melting point
Two or more substances not chemically joined
Useful mixture made to exact quantities, e.g. paint
The solvent that moves up the paper
The paper the solvent moves through
Pencil line where spots are placed at the start

walkthroughs.body_html:
In chemistry, pure means a single element or compound — nothing else.

A pure substance melts and boils at a sharp, exact temperature. A mixture melts over a range. Bottled water is a mixture; pure H2O is the chemist's meaning of pure.

A formulation is a mixture designed to do a job, with each ingredient in a measured amount.

Examples: paints, fuels, cleaning products, fertilisers, alloys, medicines. The recipe matters — change a quantity and it stops working as intended.

Draw the baseline in pencil (ink would run). Add small spots of each sample on the baseline.

Stand the paper in solvent so the level is below the baseline — otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent pool. The solvent (mobile phase) rises through the paper (stationary phase) and separates the dyes.

mcqs.q: Why is the chromatography baseline drawn in pencil?
options: Ink would dissolve and run up the paper

numericals.q: A chromatogram shows 4 distinct spots from one sample. The sample must contain at least how many substances?
